newsitem.title: USA: Sexual harassment seen as reality for U.S. teens.
newsitem.headline: Sexual harassment seen as reality for U.S. teens.

text.p: Sexual harassment is a daily reality for American teenagers and gender bias shapes their lives, according to a USA Weekend magazine survey.

The survey entitled "The Great Divide: Teens and the Gender Gap," to be published on Sept. 8, also found that parents still tended to divide home chores along traditional lines -- girls do the dishes, boys do the lawn -- and teachers were stricter with boys in school.

The survey of almost 223,000 teenagers found that three out of four have been sexually harassed, girls believe they behave more responsibly than boys -- many boys disagree -- and having a sexual relationship hurts girls more than boys.

USA Weekend said its non-scientific findings were backed by a 1996 University of Michigan study in which 83 percent of girls and 60 percent of boys said they had been sexually harassed, defined as anything from touching to being "mooned." In that study, more than half admitted to harassing others.

The magazine said its study showed that in general parents ask girls to do more of the housework and boys to do outdoor chores. Outside the home, eight of 10 said boys have more career opportunities than girls.

"Adolescents reflect what's going on in the larger society. Kids are lagging behind because teachers and parents are lagging behind. Adults talk equality but they aren't giving it everyday expression," Jim Garbarino, Cornell University's Family Life Development Centre director, was quoted as saying.

The study found, however, that 84 percent of teens were taught to believe that men and women have equal opportunities in society and more than half said they expected a woman to be elected president in their lifetime.
